name: Tyrolite Green
lede: Tyrolite Green is a bluish teal first plated by Ridgway in 1912, named for tyrolite, a copper mineral, and sold under at least nine other trade names for nearly the same color.

sections.title: A mineral teal with many aliases
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 atlas plates this color at plate VII, hue 39, tone b, a scan of an aged plate treated here as approximate [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS circular later classed it as light bluish green, 1.8 units from its block center, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary cites the same 1912 source [1]. The Munsell notation is 3.8BG 6.5/5.7 [1]. Our library's classification tags the name as a mineral word, tyrolite, a copper arsenate; beyond that the books consulted do not explain who coined the color name or when [1].

Our library also lists this exact hue under at least nine commercial names, including Aqua Sky, Beryl Green, Bridge Blue and Blue Turquoise, a sign that paint and ink makers rediscovered the same teal repeatedly under different brands [1]. The closest distinct named color on screen is [[keppel]], 3.0 units away and read as more vivid; [[verditter-blue]] and [[blue-turquoise]] both sit at 3.2, almost the same [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a rare color in our painting archive: it appears in only 0.04 percent of 23,781 paintings, 10 of them, and the within-painting lens isolates it as a dominant area in just 6, as photographed [2]. That ranks it rarer than 73 percent of the named colors we track [2]. The earliest match is a 1640 painting by Louis Le Nain, 272 years before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name; that gap marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not the pigment itself, and with only 8 dated matches the pattern is thin, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

openers: Our library lists at least nine other names — Aqua Sky, Beryl Green, Bridge Blue among them — for this same teal.
Tyrolite Green sits only 3.0 color-units from Keppel, close enough to read as the same hue.

issues: No source gives who coined the name or when, beyond the 1912 Ridgway plate.
Archive counts are very thin (n=6-10); the first-seen date is a look-alike match, not pigment evidence.
